passage: Okay, Ira, so my notebook. For two weeks I wrote bedtime, wake time, and a score out of ten for how focused I felt the next day. I expected no pattern at all. But look: on the four nights I got seven or eight hours, my focus was eight, nine, eight, nine. On the nights under six it was two, three, four. That isn't a lecture from Mum, it's my own handwriting. Something changed when I saw it. I stopped saying "I'm a night person" and started noticing that I couldn't follow chemistry after a short night. Now the notebook sits by my pillow, and the alarm goes off at the same time every day. I'm Eshaan, and I'm oddly proud of my little table.

passage:
I'm Vasudha, and I share a desk with Tanuja in Class 11. At the start of the month she started carrying a small blue notebook with columns drawn in pencil. Every morning, before assembly, she'd write in it: two times and a number.

I finally asked. She showed me: "Bed", "Up", and "Focus 1 to 5". Some days she'd slept at 1 and woken at 6:30. Focus: 2. Other days, bed at 11, up at 6:30. Focus: 4 or 5.

After two weeks she spread the pages on the desk and circled the 4s and 5s. Almost all were nights with seven or eight hours.

"I kept telling myself I work better tired," she said, tapping the page. "The notebook says I don't."

The next week I noticed she left our study group at 10:15. I can't say for sure what changed in her head. But her notebook had more 4s.

qa.q: What were the three columns in Tanuja's notebook?
What might Tanuja have felt when she saw the circled 4s and 5s?
qa.a: She may have felt surprised and a little sheepish, realising the belief that she worked better tired was wrong.

qa.q: What else could Tanuja track to understand her focus better?
qa.a: She could add a column for screen time before bed, to see whether late scrolling also affects how focused she feels.

qa.q: How does the notebook experiment look to Vasudha?
qa.a: Vasudha sees a quiet change, Tanuja leaving the study group at 10:15 and scoring more 4s, though Vasudha cannot be sure what she was thinking.

grounding: An observer describes a classmate who logs bedtime, wake time and next-day focus for two weeks and finds focus is best after enough sleep.

subtype: Approach: tracking sleep and mood in a diary [Action]
passage:
Day 1, a Monday: Jahnavi drew a simple table in the back of her rough notebook: date, when she slept, when she woke, and how well she could focus in school, from one to five. "It's just for two weeks," she told her brother Chetan, who thought it was silly.

Day 8, the next Monday: The table was filling up. Bed at 1:15, focus 2. Bed at 11, focus 4. Bed at 12:40, focus 2. She noticed she'd written "sleepy in maths" three times, always after late nights.

Day 15: She sat on the balcony with the notebook and a highlighter. Every 4 and 5 sat next to a night of seven or eight hours. Every 1 and 2 followed a short night.

"Okay," she said aloud. "It's not willpower. It's sleep."

Chetan leaned over the page. "Huh. That's actually clear." That night she was in bed by eleven, without anyone telling her.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi write three times in the table?
qa.a: "sleepy in maths", always after late nights.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi feel when she said "It's not willpower. It's sleep"?
qa.a: She felt clear-headed and convinced, perhaps relieved to have her own proof instead of just being told.

qa.q: What else could Jahnavi do with the table now?
qa.a: She could keep logging for another two weeks after the change to see whether her focus scores really rise.

qa.q: How does Chetan's view of the notebook change?
qa.a: Chetan first thought it was silly, but seeing the pattern he finds it convincing, saying it is actually clear.

grounding: Shows a student recording bedtime, wake time and next-day focus for two weeks and discovering that focus is best after enough sleep, which motivates change.
